- A way to run the project's dev command for a bounded window exists (the evidence used a PowerShell background job with a fixed sleep). If no command execution is available, stop before claiming any fix.
- Baseline crash text has been captured verbatim before changing anything, so before/after can be compared.

## Procedure
### Step 1: Confirm the failure signature
- Actions: read the full crash text; extract `code`, `syscall`, and `path`; verify `path` starts with the project's `.react-router/types`; note the Node version printed in the crash.
- Inputs: baseline crash output.
- Outputs: confirmed `ENOTEMPTY`/`rmdir` or `EPERM`/`scandir` signature under `.react-router/types`.
- Cautions: PowerShell prefixes Node stderr with `CategoryInfo`/`FullyQualifiedErrorId` noise — the real error is the `[Error: ...] { errno, code, syscall, path }` block.
- Preserve: the original crash text for the before/after comparison.
- Next: signature matches → Step 2; otherwise stop and treat as a different problem.

### Step 2: Establish that the folder is locked at the OS level (inspection only)
- Actions: list the folder with `cmd /c "dir /a <path>"` to see whether it is empty; note whether POSIX-style listing reports `Permission denied`.
- Inputs: the `path` from Step 1.
- Outputs: knowledge that the folder may show `0 File(s)` yet be undeletable — which routes the fix to Step 3 instead of deletion.
- Cautions: do NOT spend attempts on `rm -rf`, `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`, `cmd rd /s /q`, `node fs.rmSync`, `takeown`/`icacls`, or `robocopy /MIR`; the evidence shows every one of them failing on this kind of volume (see Common Failures).
- Preserve: the directory itself — leave it in place; the patched cleanup tolerates it.
- Next: empty-but-locked → Step 3; deletable → delete normally and re-run dev instead (no patch needed).

### Step 3: Locate the cleanup call in `@react-router/dev`
- Actions: grep `typesDirectory` across `node_modules/@react-router/dev/dist`; confirm the awaited cleanup line `await import_promises.default.rm(typesDirectory(ctx), { recursive: true, force: true });` in `dist/vite.js` (`watch`) and in `dist/cli/index.js` (both `run` and `watch`).
- Inputs: `node_modules/@react-router/dev/dist`.
- Outputs: a file/line list of every occurrence (evidence: one in `vite.js`, two in `cli/index.js`).
- Cautions: `grep` for `EPERM|scandir` finds nothing — the crash comes from Node's `fs/promises.rm`, not from app code; search for `typesDirectory` instead.
- Preserve: do not edit surrounding logic.
- Next: at least one occurrence found → Step 4; none found → stop and report that the source layout differs.

### Step 4: Neutralize the cleanup failure at every occurrence
- Actions: append `.catch(() => {})` to the awaited `rm(...)` call so the cleanup promise can never reject; apply to all occurrences from Step 3.
- Inputs: occurrence list.
- Outputs: patched `dist/vite.js` and `dist/cli/index.js`.
- Cautions: `force: true` does not suppress these errors — do not rely on it; the only change is the appended catch.
- Preserve: every other byte of the files; keep the patch one-line-per-site so it is easy to re-apply.
- Next: Step 5.

### Step 5: Verify with a bounded dev-server run
- Actions: start the project's dev command in a background job, wait a fixed window (evidence: 8–12 seconds), capture output, then stop the job (PowerShell pattern: `Start-Job` → `Start-Sleep` → `Receive-Job` → `Stop-Job`/`Remove-Job`).
- Inputs: patched project.
- Outputs: captured startup log.
- Cautions: a rejected/cancelled tool call means verification did not happen; background-job output mixes npm wrapper noise with the real error — search for `ENOTEMPTY` and `EPERM` explicitly.
- Next: no `ENOTEMPTY`/`EPERM` and typegen progressed → Step 6; crash persists → Common Failures; run never executed → report "patched, unverified".

### Step 6: Record the re-apply requirement
- Actions: state that the patch exists only in `node_modules` and is wiped by any `npm install`; save the exact lines to patch so a future session can redo Step 4 quickly.
- Inputs: patched line list.
- Outputs: re-apply note.
- Cautions: a later full deletion of `.react-router` from Bash did succeed once in the evidence after the earlier failures; the reason the lock cleared is 轨迹未提供 — do not rely on it.
- Next: done.

## Decision Rules
### When the crash `path` is under `.react-router/types` with `syscall: rmdir` or `scandir`
Go straight to source-level handling (Step 3): the failing call is React Router's typegen cleanup, not application code.

### When every deletion tool fails (`Access is denied`, `Directory not empty`, `ERROR 5`)
Stop deleting. The folder can be empty per `cmd dir /a` and still be undeletable; deletion attempts on this class of volume were all failures in the evidence — route to Steps 3–4.

### When `takeown` reports no ACL support
Abandon ownership/ACL fixes entirely (`icacls`, grants, take ownership); the volume reports that ACLs are unsupported, so no permission change will succeed.

### When grep for `typesDirectory` returns multiple `rm(...)` occurrences
Patch all of them: the dev server path goes through `watch()` in `dist/vite.js`, and one-off/CLI typegen goes through `run()` and `watch()` in `dist/cli/index.js`.

### When the verification run is rejected, cancelled, or impossible
Report the outcome as "patched, unverified" and hand over the exact re-run command; never summarize it as fixed.

### When the error path is not under `.react-router/types`, or the directory deletes fine
This skill does not apply — no patch is warranted.

## Invariants
- Only `node_modules/@react-router/dev` files are modified; no project source, route, or config file is changed to work around the crash.
- Nothing outside the `.react-router` cache is deleted, and no deletion at all happens once the OS-level lock is confirmed.
- The patch is additive and minimal — appending `.catch(() => {})` to the cleanup call, changing nothing else — so it can be re-applied identically after a reinstall.
- No success is reported without an observed clean re-run of the dev command; a rejected or missing verification run leaves the state "patched, unverified".
- PowerShell's `NativeCommandError`/`CategoryInfo` wrapper text is treated as noise, not as the error under diagnosis; the `code`/`syscall`/`path` block is the source of truth.
- The locked directory itself is left in place for the patched cleanup to tolerate; it is not renamed, moved, or chown'ed.

## Common Failures
### Failure: recursive deletion of the types cache fails
- Symptoms: `rm: cannot remove '/<path>/.react-router/types/app/routes': Directory not empty`; `cmd rmdir` → `Access is denied`; `robocopy /MIR` → `ERROR 5 (0x00000005) Deleting Extra Directory ... Access is denied`; Node `fs.rmSync` → `EPERM ... scandir`.
- Causes: the `+types` subfolders are empty per `cmd dir /a` yet undeletable on this volume; the exact origin of the lock is 轨迹未提供 (not confirmed in the evidence).
- Recovery: stop deleting (Step 2) and patch the cleanup call (Steps 3–4); the patched cleanup tolerates a leftover folder.

### Failure: ownership/ACL tools refuse to run
- Symptoms: `ERROR: File ownership cannot be applied on insecure file systems;` and `there is no support for ACLs.`; `icacls` parameter errors.
- Causes: the volume does not support ACLs, so no grant/ownership change is possible.
- Recovery: drop `takeown`/`icacls` from the plan; proceed to the source patch.

### Failure: `EPERM scandir` on a second `+types` path after partial cleanup
- Symptoms: after some directories are removed, the next start crashes with `EPERM: operation not permitted, scandir '<...>/types/app/+types'`.
- Causes: more than one locked folder exists; each cleanup attempt surfaces them one at a time.
- Recovery: the same patch covers it — `fs.promises.rm` on the types directory is the single choke point; no per-folder work is needed.

### Failure: the patch silently disappears
- Symptoms: the original `ENOTEMPTY` crash returns after dependency work.
- Causes: `npm install` regenerated `node_modules`, discarding the edited dist files.
- Recovery: re-run Steps 3–4; keep the recorded line list so re-application is mechanical.

### Failure: reported as fixed without a run
- Symptoms: a summary claims the dev server works while the verification tool call was rejected/cancelled, so no post-patch output exists.
- Causes: verification skipped or interrupted.
- Recovery: re-run Step 5 before making any success claim; otherwise state "patched, unverified".

## Verification
Observable checks (do not mark as done unless each has tool output behind it):

- Baseline captured: the pre-fix crash text containing `ENOTEMPTY: directory not empty` or `EPERM: operation not permitted, scandir` with a `path` under `.react-router/types` is saved for comparison.
- Read-back of patched lines: re-read `dist/vite.js` around the `watch()` cleanup and `dist/cli/index.js` around `run()`/`watch()`; every `await import_promises.default.rm(typesDirectory(ctx), { recursive: true, force: true })` line now ends in `.catch(() => {});`.
- Coverage: grep for `rm(typesDirectory` returns only `.catch(() => {});`-terminated lines (count matches the pre-patch occurrence list).
- Bounded dev run: background start + fixed wait + captured output contains neither `ENOTEMPTY` nor `EPERM`, and shows typegen progressing (e.g. `generated types`).
- Blast radius: `git status`/file listing shows changes only under `node_modules/@react-router/dev` — no project source or config edits.
- Re-apply note written, stating the patch is lost on the next `npm install`.

Explicitly NOT established by the source trace: the post-patch dev run was rejected before executing, so in that session only the diagnosis and the edits were verified. Any claim beyond "patched" requires a fresh run of the check above.

## Examples
### Example 1: dev server dies on startup with ENOTEMPTY
- Input: Windows project; `npm run dev` output ends with `Error: ENOTEMPTY: directory not empty, rmdir '<root>\.react-router\types\app\routes'` (Node.js v22.20.0).
- Procedure: Step 1 (signature under `.react-router/types`) → Step 2 (`cmd dir /a` shows the folder empty; deletion ruled out) → Step 3 (grep `typesDirectory` finds the cleanup in `dist/vite.js` watch and `dist/cli/index.js` run/watch) → Step 4 (append `.catch(() => {})` at all three sites) → Step 5 (bounded background dev run) → Step 6 (re-apply note).
- Expected result: the bounded run shows no `ENOTEMPTY`/`EPERM` and typegen proceeds; only the three `node_modules` lines differ from baseline. In the source trace this final run was rejected by the user, so that session's honest status is "patched, unverified".
- Parameterized values: project root (`<root>`), package dist layout (`node_modules/@react-router/dev/dist`), Node version (v22.20.0 in evidence), sleep window (8–12 s).

### Example 2: deletion already ruled out, go straight to the patch
- Input: `cmd /c "dir /a ...+types"` reports `0 File(s)` while `ls` returns `Permission denied` and `robocopy /MIR` exits with `ERROR 5 (0x00000005) Deleting Extra Directory ... Access is denied`.
- Procedure: skip repeated deletion attempts; Step 3 → Step 4 → Step 5.
- Expected result: cleanup call neutralized; the locked folder remains in place and the next start does not crash on it.
- Parameterized values: locked subpaths (`app/+types`, `app/routes/+types`), the exact dist files present in the installed `@react-router/dev` build.

skill:fix-windows-stack-overflow-in-larg.name: fix-windows-stack-overflow-in-large-local-fixtures
skill:fix-windows-stack-overflow-in-larg.description: Use when a Windows test executable prints no output (or partial output) and exits with -1073741571 (0xC00000FD) even though it linked successfully. Helps the agent identify large fixed-size structs allocated as local/by-value variables that blow the 1 MB default stack, move them to static storage or references, and re-run the suite to green. Requires a Windows test build (clang++/PowerShell) and the ability to edit test sources. Do not use for LNK1105/link failures or for assertion-level test failures that print FAIL lines.
skill:fix-windows-stack-overflow-in-larg.body:
# Fix Windows Test Binaries That Crash Silently with Exit -1073741571

## Goal
Make Windows test executables that crash before printing anything (observed exit `-1073741571`, i.e. `0xC00000FD` stack overflow) run to completion by relocating oversized fixed-size fixture structs off the call stack, verified by the suite printing its full pass counts.

## Scope
### In scope
- Windows test/CLI binaries that link successfully but terminate immediately with no output or exit code `-1073741571` (`0xC00000FD`, STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW).
- Test fixtures and harness structs that embed large fixed-capacity tables (atom tables, clause databases, term arenas, registries) declared as local variables or returned/assigned by value.
- Moving such state to static storage (class static members or function-local `static`) or to references so it lives in BSS/heap rather than on the 1 MB default Windows thread stack.
- Re-running the affected suite(s) to confirm normal output and exit code 0.

### Out of scope
- Link failures (`LNK1105` and other linker errors) — handle the lock problem instead.
- Test assertion failures that print `FAIL` lines with a nonzero exit — those are logic defects.
- Production code stack-usage redesign beyond test fixtures (not observed/verified here).
- Increasing thread stack size via linker/`CreateThread` parameters (not observed in the trace; not a verified remedy).

## Inputs
- **Crash signature**: tool result showing the test binary producing no output (or truncated output) and `exit: -1073741571`; source = the run of the built `.exe`; required = yes; constraint = link must have succeeded (no `LNK1105`); default = 无.
- **Test source file**: the `.cpp`/`.c` defining the fixture context struct (e.g. `tests/test_indexing.cpp`, `tests/test_atoms.cpp`); source = identified from the test name in the crash output; required = yes; constraint = edit only test files; default = 无.
- **Fixture struct definition**: struct declaration whose members are large fixed-size tables (`AtomTable`, `Database`, `TermArena`, `VarRegistry`); source = reading the test file; required = yes; constraint = size must plausibly exceed the 1 MB Windows default stack; default = 无.
- **Existing pattern to copy**: a working test that already stores the same state in `static` members (e.g. `test_solver.cpp` with `static Database s_db`); source = project test code; required = no; constraint = reuse the project's established pattern rather than inventing a new one; default = 无.
- **Build/run command**: the command that compiles and runs the suite (PowerShell loop invoking `clang++ ... -o <exe>` then `& <exe>`); source = the failed run's tool call; required = yes; constraint = re-run unchanged after the edit; default = 无.
- **Expected counts**: per-suite pass totals (e.g. `13/13 tests passed`); source = earlier runs of the same suite where available; required = no; constraint = use the suite's own printed totals; default = 无.

## Outputs
### Artifacts
- **Edited test source** (e.g. `tests/test_indexing.cpp`) where the fixture's large members are `static` (class static members or function-local `static`) or held by reference instead of by value.
- **Rebuilt test executable** at its original output path.
- **Run log** showing the suite's full output and pass counts with exit code 0.

### Success criteria
- The suite prints its complete per-test output and a pass summary (e.g. `13/13 tests passed`) with exit `0`; no `-1073741571` appears.
- The whole test run reports all expected suites passing (observed: `FINAL RESULT: 10/10 suites passed, 0 failed`).
- No production source, build flags, or linker settings were changed to achieve this.

### Failure criteria
- The binary still exits `-1073741571` after the state was moved off the stack.
- The suite runs but reports `FAIL` assertions — a logic defect, report separately.
- The link fails with `LNK1105` — out of scope; switch to the lock-handling workflow.

## Preconditions
- The binary must link successfully first; if the run log contains `LNK1105`, stop and resolve the output-file lock before diagnosing crashes.
- The crash must be silent/abrupt: no test output at all, or output stopping before that suite's header, with exit `-1073741571`. If the suite prints `FAIL` lines, this skill does not apply.
- The host must be Windows (the `-1073741571` / 1 MB default stack behavior is Windows-specific), with the project's compiler (`clang++`) and shell (PowerShell) available for rebuild-and-rerun.
- The fixture struct and its member types must be readable and editable (test sources); confirm which struct the test instantiates as a local before editing.
- A prior or sibling run of the suite should exist (or be runnable) to establish the expected output/counts for comparison.

## Procedure
### Step 1: Confirm the silent-crash signature
- Actions: run the suite binary (or read the last run) and confirm: link succeeded, then the process exits `-1073741571` with no (or truncated) output.
- Inputs: run log for the suspect test executable.
- Outputs: confirmation of stack-overflow-style abrupt exit; note which suite header never printed.
- Cautions: PowerShell may swallow child output on crash — capture `$LASTEXITCODE` explicitly; a missing `.exe` or `LNK1105` means the wrong problem.
- Preserve: the existing binary/run command for before/after comparison.
- Next: proceed to Step 2 when exit is `-1073741571` and the link was clean.

### Step 2: Locate the oversized local fixture
- Actions: open the test source; find the per-test context struct instantiated as a local in each test case (e.g. `struct IdxCtx { AtomTable atoms; Database db; TermArena clause_arena; ... };`); estimate its size from member arrays (atom tables ~1 MB, clause databases with per-predicate indexes ~1.6 MB, arenas/registries hundreds of KB).
- Inputs: test source file; member type definitions if sizes are unclear.
- Outputs: the struct name, the members that dominate its size, and the local-instantiation sites.
- Cautions: a multi-MB struct created once per test case sequentially still overflows a 1 MB stack if it is a stack local; do not assume "only one at a time" is safe.
- Preserve: the struct's semantics (same members, same init sequence).
- Next: proceed to Step 3 when the local and its big members are identified.

### Step 3: Move the state off the call stack
- Actions: prefer the project's existing pattern — make the big members `static` (class static members defined at namespace scope, as an existing passing test already does with `static Database s_db`, or function-local `static`); if the value is produced by a function returning a large struct by value, change the use to a reference/pointer instead of a copy (e.g. `AtomTable &t = make_table();`).
- Inputs: fixture struct definition; existing static-member pattern in a passing sibling test.
- Outputs: edited test source.
- Cautions: static members are shared across all test cases in the binary — each test must still re-initialize state in its constructor/setup exactly as before, or earlier tests will pollute later ones; keep the edits inside test files.
- Preserve: member order, initialization calls, and test assertions unchanged.
- Next: rebuild and rerun (Step 4).

### Step 4: Rebuild the binary with the unchanged command and run it
- Actions: re-run the project's compile-and-link command for that suite (same flags, same `-o` path), then execute the binary and capture `$LASTEXITCODE`.
- Inputs: build/run command from Step 1.
- Outputs: fresh link log and full suite output.
- Cautions: if `LNK1105` appears now, the binary is locked by a prior run — kill/rename per the lock workflow, then retry; do not confuse it with the crash.
- Preserve: all compiler flags and the output path.
- Next: proceed to Verification when the suite prints output; iterate on Step 3 if the crash persists.

### Step 5: Run the whole test batch
- Actions: run every suite in the project's test loop to confirm no regression elsewhere after the fixture change.
- Inputs: full test loop command.
- Outputs: aggregate pass/fail summary across suites.
- Cautions: suites that previously crashed silently may now run and reveal real assertion failures — report those separately as logic issues.
- Preserve: test order and flags.
- Next: stop when all suites pass; otherwise triage each failure by type (crash vs FAIL).

## Decision Rules
### When the binary exits `-1073741571` with no output after a clean link
Treat as `0xC00000FD` stack overflow in process startup/first test; inspect the test fixture struct for large fixed-capacity locals rather than debugging assertions or the linker.

### When the fixture struct's members include multi-MB fixed tables instantiated as function locals
Make the members `static` (class static members or function-local `static`) so they are zero-initialized in BSS before `main`, and keep per-test `init` calls in the constructor/setup. Observed: a context struct with a ~1 MB atom table plus a ~1.6 MB database crashed as a local and passed after becoming static members.

### When a helper returns a large struct by value into a local
Change the call site to bind a reference (or pointer) instead of copying; observed fix: `AtomTable t = make_table()` → `AtomTable &t = make_table()` for a ~1 MB struct copied onto the stack.

### When a freshly linked binary under a new filename still crashes with the same exit code
The lock workaround is irrelevant to the crash — proceed with the stack fix; do not keep producing new filenames expecting different behavior.

### When the suite runs after the fix but prints `FAIL` lines
Stop the stack-overflow work; the crash is resolved and the remaining failures are assertion/logic defects to be handled separately (observed: unrelated solver backtracking failures surfaced once binaries ran).

### When the suspect state is a class static member already
Class statics with trivial default constructors live in BSS and do not consume stack — if a static-member test still crashes, look for a different large local (e.g. a by-value copy) instead of making more members static.

## Invariants
- Edit only test files (and only the fixture/storage declarations); do not change production sources, compiler flags, linker settings, or build scripts to work around a test stack overflow.
- Keep the fixture's member set, initialization order, and per-test reset behavior identical — only the storage duration/location changes.
- Do not weaken, skip, or delete tests to make the suite green; assertions must remain as-is.
- Do not report a suite as passing without its own printed pass counts and exit 0 from a run after the edit.
- Do not keep relinking under new filenames to dodge a crash — filename changes never alter stack usage.
- Distinguish the three failure classes (link lock LNK1105, stack-overflow crash `-1073741571`, assertion `FAIL`) and never claim one fixed another.
- Preserve the project's existing conventions (e.g. reuse the static-instance helper pattern already present in sibling tests) instead of introducing a new framework.

## Common Failures
### Failure: suite prints nothing and exits -1073741571
- Symptoms: `=== <suite> ===` header prints from the harness, then immediately `exit: -1073741571` (or the header itself never appears); no PASS/FAIL lines.
- Causes: a multi-MB fixed-size fixture struct instantiated as a function-local variable, or a by-value copy of such a struct, exceeding the 1 MB default Windows stack before the first assertion runs.
- Recovery: make the fixture members `static` (class statics or function-local `static`) or bind references instead of copies, rebuild with the same command, rerun.

### Failure: suite runs but a single test copies a large struct by value
- Symptoms: most tests print, but the process dies partway (or a specific test never reports) with the same crash code.
- Causes: one remaining `BigStruct t = make_table();`-style value copy among otherwise reference-based tests (observed at `test_atoms.cpp` line 108 while every other test used `&t`).
- Recovery: change that single copy to a reference (`AtomTable &t = make_table();`) and rerun.

### Failure: converted fixture makes later tests fail with wrong state
- Symptoms: after moving to `static`, some tests fail assertions that previously passed.
- Causes: static storage is shared across all test cases in the binary; missing per-test re-initialization lets earlier tests pollute later ones.
- Recovery: keep/restore the constructor or helper's `*_init(...)` calls on every test entry (the observed pattern re-initialized inside the static-instance helper on each call).

### Failure: relink reports LNK1105 instead of running
- Symptoms: after the source edit, the build fails with `LNK1105 ... error code 1224`.
- Causes: a previous run of the binary is still alive or its handle is held.

---
name: fix-windows-stack-overflow-in-large-local-fixtures
description: Use when a Windows test executable prints no output (or partial output) and exits with -1073741571 (0xC00000FD) even though it linked successfully. Helps the agent identify large fixed-size structs allocated as local/by-value variables that blow the 1 MB default stack, move them to static storage or references, and re-run the suite to green. Requires a Windows test build (clang++/PowerShell) and the ability to edit test sources. Do not use for LNK1105/link failures or for assertion-level test failures that print FAIL lines.
triggers:
  - "-1073741571"
  - "0xC00000FD"
  - "STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW"
---
# Fix Windows Test Binaries That Crash Silently with Exit -1073741571

## Goal
Make Windows test executables that crash before printing anything (observed exit `-1073741571`, i.e. `0xC00000FD` stack overflow) run to completion by relocating oversized fixed-size fixture structs off the call stack, verified by the suite printing its full pass counts.

## Scope
### In scope
- Windows test/CLI binaries that link successfully but terminate immediately with no output or exit code `-1073741571` (`0xC00000FD`, STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW).
- Test fixtures and harness structs that embed large fixed-capacity tables (atom tables, clause databases, term arenas, registries) declared as local variables or returned/assigned by value.
- Moving such state to static storage (class static members or function-local `static`) or to references so it lives in BSS/heap rather than on the 1 MB default Windows thread stack.
- Re-running the affected suite(s) to confirm normal output and exit code 0.

### Out of scope
- Link failures (`LNK1105` and other linker errors) — handle the lock problem instead.
- Test assertion failures that print `FAIL` lines with a nonzero exit — those are logic defects.
- Production code stack-usage redesign beyond test fixtures (not observed/verified here).
- Increasing thread stack size via linker/`CreateThread` parameters (not observed in the trace; not a verified remedy).

## Inputs
- **Crash signature**: tool result showing the test binary producing no output (or truncated output) and `exit: -1073741571`; source = the run of the built `.exe`; required = yes; constraint = link must have succeeded (no `LNK1105`); default = 无.
- **Test source file**: the `.cpp`/`.c` defining the fixture context struct (e.g. `tests/test_indexing.cpp`, `tests/test_atoms.cpp`); source = identified from the test name in the crash output; required = yes; constraint = edit only test files; default = 无.
- **Fixture struct definition**: struct declaration whose members are large fixed-size tables (`AtomTable`, `Database`, `TermArena`, `VarRegistry`); source = reading the test file; required = yes; constraint = size must plausibly exceed the 1 MB Windows default stack; default = 无.
- **Existing pattern to copy**: a working test that already stores the same state in `static` members (e.g. `test_solver.cpp` with `static Database s_db`); source = project test code; required = no; constraint = reuse the project's established pattern rather than inventing a new one; default = 无.
- **Build/run command**: the command that compiles and runs the suite (PowerShell loop invoking `clang++ ... -o <exe>` then `& <exe>`); source = the failed run's tool call; required = yes; constraint = re-run unchanged after the edit; default = 无.
- **Expected counts**: per-suite pass totals (e.g. `13/13 tests passed`); source = earlier runs of the same suite where available; required = no; constraint = use the suite's own printed totals; default = 无.

## Outputs
### Artifacts
- **Edited test source** (e.g. `tests/test_indexing.cpp`) where the fixture's large members are `static` (class static members or function-local `static`) or held by reference instead of by value.
- **Rebuilt test executable** at its original output path.
- **Run log** showing the suite's full output and pass counts with exit code 0.

### Success criteria
- The suite prints its complete per-test output and a pass summary (e.g. `13/13 tests passed`) with exit `0`; no `-1073741571` appears.
- The whole test run reports all expected suites passing (observed: `FINAL RESULT: 10/10 suites passed, 0 failed`).
- No production source, build flags, or linker settings were changed to achieve this.

### Failure criteria
- The binary still exits `-1073741571` after the state was moved off the stack.
- The suite runs but reports `FAIL` assertions — a logic defect, report separately.
- The link fails with `LNK1105` — out of scope; switch to the lock-handling workflow.

## Preconditions
- The binary must link successfully first; if the run log contains `LNK1105`, stop and resolve the output-file lock before diagnosing crashes.
- The crash must be silent/abrupt: no test output at all, or output stopping before that suite's header, with exit `-1073741571`. If the suite prints `FAIL` lines, this skill does not apply.
- The host must be Windows (the `-1073741571` / 1 MB default stack behavior is Windows-specific), with the project's compiler (`clang++`) and shell (PowerShell) available for rebuild-and-rerun.
- The fixture struct and its member types must be readable and editable (test sources); confirm which struct the test instantiates as a local before editing.
- A prior or sibling run of the suite should exist (or be runnable) to establish the expected output/counts for comparison.

## Procedure
### Step 1: Confirm the silent-crash signature
- Actions: run the suite binary (or read the last run) and confirm: link succeeded, then the process exits `-1073741571` with no (or truncated) output.
- Inputs: run log for the suspect test executable.
- Outputs: confirmation of stack-overflow-style abrupt exit; note which suite header never printed.
- Cautions: PowerShell may swallow child output on crash — capture `$LASTEXITCODE` explicitly; a missing `.exe` or `LNK1105` means the wrong problem.
- Preserve: the existing binary/run command for before/after comparison.
- Next: proceed to Step 2 when exit is `-1073741571` and the link was clean.

### Step 2: Locate the oversized local fixture
- Actions: open the test source; find the per-test context struct instantiated as a local in each test case (e.g. `struct IdxCtx { AtomTable atoms; Database db; TermArena clause_arena; ... };`); estimate its size from member arrays (atom tables ~1 MB, clause databases with per-predicate indexes ~1.6 MB, arenas/registries hundreds of KB).
- Inputs: test source file; member type definitions if sizes are unclear.
- Outputs: the struct name, the members that dominate its size, and the local-instantiation sites.
- Cautions: a multi-MB struct created once per test case sequentially still overflows a 1 MB stack if it is a stack local; do not assume "only one at a time" is safe.
- Preserve: the struct's semantics (same members, same init sequence).
- Next: proceed to Step 3 when the local and its big members are identified.

### Step 3: Move the state off the call stack
- Actions: prefer the project's existing pattern — make the big members `static` (class static members defined at namespace scope, as an existing passing test already does with `static Database s_db`, or function-local `static`); if the value is produced by a function returning a large struct by value, change the use to a reference/pointer instead of a copy (e.g. `AtomTable &t = make_table();`).
- Inputs: fixture struct definition; existing static-member pattern in a passing sibling test.
- Outputs: edited test source.
- Cautions: static members are shared across all test cases in the binary — each test must still re-initialize state in its constructor/setup exactly as before, or earlier tests will pollute later ones; keep the edits inside test files.
- Preserve: member order, initialization calls, and test assertions unchanged.
- Next: rebuild and rerun (Step 4).

### Step 4: Rebuild the binary with the unchanged command and run it
- Actions: re-run the project's compile-and-link command for that suite (same flags, same `-o` path), then execute the binary and capture `$LASTEXITCODE`.
- Inputs: build/run command from Step 1.
- Outputs: fresh link log and full suite output.
- Cautions: if `LNK1105` appears now, the binary is locked by a prior run — kill/rename per the lock workflow, then retry; do not confuse it with the crash.
- Preserve: all compiler flags and the output path.
- Next: proceed to Verification when the suite prints output; iterate on Step 3 if the crash persists.

### Step 5: Run the whole test batch
- Actions: run every suite in the project's test loop to confirm no regression elsewhere after the fixture change.
- Inputs: full test loop command.
- Outputs: aggregate pass/fail summary across suites.
- Cautions: suites that previously crashed silently may now run and reveal real assertion failures — report those separately as logic issues.
- Preserve: test order and flags.
- Next: stop when all suites pass; otherwise triage each failure by type (crash vs FAIL).

## Decision Rules
### When the binary exits `-1073741571` with no output after a clean link
Treat as `0xC00000FD` stack overflow in process startup/first test; inspect the test fixture struct for large fixed-capacity locals rather than debugging assertions or the linker.

### When the fixture struct's members include multi-MB fixed tables instantiated as function locals
Make the members `static` (class static members or function-local `static`) so they are zero-initialized in BSS before `main`, and keep per-test `init` calls in the constructor/setup. Observed: a context struct with a ~1 MB atom table plus a ~1.6 MB database crashed as a local and passed after becoming static members.

### When a helper returns a large struct by value into a local
Change the call site to bind a reference (or pointer) instead of copying; observed fix: `AtomTable t = make_table()` → `AtomTable &t = make_table()` for a ~1 MB struct copied onto the stack.

### When a freshly linked binary under a new filename still crashes with the same exit code
The lock workaround is irrelevant to the crash — proceed with the stack fix; do not keep producing new filenames expecting different behavior.

### When the suite runs after the fix but prints `FAIL` lines
Stop the stack-overflow work; the crash is resolved and the remaining failures are assertion/logic defects to be handled separately (observed: unrelated solver backtracking failures surfaced once binaries ran).

### When the suspect state is a class static member already
Class statics with trivial default constructors live in BSS and do not consume stack — if a static-member test still crashes, look for a different large local (e.g. a by-value copy) instead of making more members static.

- Edit only test files (and only the fixture/storage declarations); do not change production sources, compiler flags, linker settings, or build scripts to work around a test stack overflow.
- Keep the fixture's member set, initialization order, and per-test reset behavior identical — only the storage duration/location changes.
- Do not weaken, skip, or delete tests to make the suite green; assertions must remain as-is.
- Do not report a suite as passing without its own printed pass counts and exit 0 from a run after the edit.
- Do not keep relinking under new filenames to dodge a crash — filename changes never alter stack usage.
- Distinguish the three failure classes (link lock LNK1105, stack-overflow crash `-1073741571`, assertion `FAIL`) and never claim one fixed another.
- Preserve the project's existing conventions (e.g. reuse the static-instance helper pattern already present in sibling tests) instead of introducing a new framework.

- Causes: a multi-MB fixed-size fixture struct instantiated as a function-local variable, or a by-value copy of such a struct, exceeding the 1 MB default Windows stack before the first assertion runs.
- Recovery: make the fixture members `static` (class statics or function-local `static`) or bind references instead of copies, rebuild with the same command, rerun.

# Resolve LNK1105 "cannot close file" Output Locks on Windows

## Goal
Diagnose and clear a Windows link failure reported as `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file '<output>'; error code 1224`, so the project's normal build command links the intended output binary successfully and the produced binary can be executed.

## Scope
### In scope
- Windows link failures whose message is exactly `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file '<path>'; error code 1224` (MSVC `link.exe` invoked through clang/clang++/clang-cl, `make`, `.bat` build scripts, or PowerShell build loops).
- Identifying which running process holds the output `.exe` (by image name or by full path).
- Releasing the lock by terminating the holding process, waiting for handle release, force-deleting the output file, or — as an unblock workaround — relinking to a fresh output filename.
- Confirming the original build command then links and the binary runs.

### Out of scope
- Link errors other than LNK1105/1224 (undefined symbols, missing object files, LNK1123/LNK1104 media errors).
- Source-code or compiler-flag problems; compilation of `.c/.cpp` objects (these already succeeded in every observed case).
- Linux/macOS build environments and non-Windows error codes.
- Runtime crashes of the produced binary that occur after a successful link (those are separate failures).

## Inputs
- **Failing build output**: text of the failed link step; source = the shell/tool result that contained `LNK1105` and `error code 1224`; required = yes; constraint = must name the output file path (e.g. `bin\yggdrasil.exe`, `build\frost_smoke.exe`); default = 无.
- **Locked output path**: the `.exe` path quoted in the LNK1105 message; source = parsed from the error line; required = yes; constraint = used verbatim for deletion/existence checks; default = 无.
- **Output binary image name**: file name without directory (e.g. `yggdrasil.exe` → process name `yggdrasil`); source = derived from the locked output path; required = yes; constraint = process names on Windows omit the `.exe` suffix in `Stop-Process -Name`; default = 无.
- **Build command**: the exact command that produced the failure (`make`, `.\build.bat run`, direct `clang++ ... -o <out>`); source = the failed tool call; required = yes; constraint = must be re-run unchanged after the lock is cleared; default = 无.
- **Shell environment**: PowerShell or Git-Bash on Windows; source = observed session shell; required = yes; constraint = PowerShell uses `Stop-Process`/`Get-Process`/`Remove-Item`, Bash uses `taskkill`/`sleep`; default = 无.
- **Post-lock delay**: wait before relink; source = 无 (operator choice); required = no; constraint = observed working values 300–1000 ms; default = 500 ms.
- **Fresh output filename** (workaround only): alternative `-o` target such as `test_solver2025.exe`; source = 无 (operator choice); required = no; constraint = only unblocks running under a new name; does not satisfy a build system that expects the canonical name; default = 无.

## Outputs
### Artifacts
- **Rebuilt output binary** at the original output path (e.g. `bin\yggdrasil.exe`, `build\frost_smoke.exe`), format = PE executable produced by the project's own link command.
- **Relink log** (tool result text) showing the link command completing without `LNK1105`.
- **Optional workaround binary** under a fresh name (e.g. `build\tests\test_solver2025.exe`), only if the fresh-name branch was used.

### Success criteria
- The original build command exits with the success status of that build system and its output contains no `LNK1105` / `error code 1224`.
- The output `.exe` exists at the expected path and (when the original task requires it) launches and produces its normal output.

### Failure criteria
- `LNK1105 ... error code 1224` still appears after the remediation steps.
- The binary exists but crashes or exits abnormally when run — this is a separate runtime problem, not an LNK1105 resolution.
- A process was terminated that was not matched to the locked output (unintended collateral kill).

## Preconditions
- The failing output must show both `LNK1105` and `error code 1224`; if either is absent, stop and diagnose the actual linker error instead.
- All compilation steps must already succeed — object files (`.o`) build cleanly and only the final link fails. If compilation also fails, fix that first.
- The shell must be Windows-capable with permission to terminate processes and delete files in the build directory (PowerShell `Stop-Process` / `Get-Process` / `Remove-Item`, or Git-Bash `taskkill`); without process-kill permission, fall back to the fresh-filename branch only.
- The exact original build command must be recoverable from the failed tool call so the identical command can be re-run for verification.
- A process-kill or file-delete must be authorized in the session; if the environment forbids killing processes, report the blocker instead of guessing at source-level "fixes".

## Procedure
### Step 1: Confirm the failure signature
- Actions: read the failed build output; require the line `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file '<path>'; error code 1224` and note the exact output path.
- Inputs: failed tool result text.
- Outputs: locked output path, output image name (without `.exe` for `Stop-Process -Name`).
- Cautions: compilation lines preceding the error are context only — they succeeded; do not change compiler flags or sources.
- Preserve: the original build command verbatim for Step 4.
- Next: proceed to Step 2 when both LNK1105 and 1224 are present; otherwise stop and handle the real error.

### Step 2: Find and terminate the process holding the output
- Actions: kill processes by expected image name first, e.g. PowerShell `Stop-Process -Name yggdrasil -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, or Bash `taskkill /F /IM frost_smoke.exe /IM frost_subsystems.exe 2>/dev/null`. If the name-based kill finds nothing or the lock persists, enumerate by path pattern, e.g. `Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*dmls*' -or $_.Name -like '*dmls*' } | Stop-Process -Force -EA 0`, then kill it.
- Inputs: output image name; shell type.
- Outputs: a process list (possibly empty) and terminated matching processes.
- Cautions: `Stop-Process -Name x -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` prints nothing when no such process exists — an empty result does not prove the lock is gone; check the file before relinking.
- Preserve: only processes whose name/path matches the locked output; never a blanket `Stop-Process` of everything.
- Next: proceed to Step 3.

### Step 3: Short wait, then verify the file handle is releasable
- Actions: sleep briefly (`Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500` / `sleep 1`), then optionally test deletability with `Remove-Item -Force <path> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` and check `$?`, or check existence with `[System.IO.File]::Exists('<path>')`.
- Inputs: locked output path.
- Outputs: whether the output file can now be deleted / exists.
- Cautions: Windows may keep the handle a moment after process exit — an immediate relink can still fail even after a successful kill.
- Preserve: if `Remove-Item` returns `True`, the file is gone; the build system will recreate it.
- Next: proceed to Step 4; if deletion fails and no matching process exists, use the Step 5 workaround.

### Step 4: Re-run the identical build command
- Actions: re-run the exact command from Step 1 (e.g. `make`, `.\build.bat run`, or the direct `clang++ ... -o <out>` line).
- Inputs: original build command.
- Outputs: new link log.
- Cautions: one retry immediately after a kill may still report LNK1105; retry once more after another ~1 s wait before escalating.
- Preserve: all flags, object lists, and output paths unchanged — this is verification of the lock fix, not a build-system refactor.
- Next: if the log contains no LNK1105 and the build's success message appears, go to Verification; if it still fails, go to Step 5.

### Step 5 (workaround): Link to a fresh output filename
- Actions: when the canonical output must stay locked or the lock cannot be cleared, relink with a different `-o` target (e.g. `build\tests\test_solver2025.exe`, `build\tests\test_indexing2025.exe`) using the same sources and objects; run that binary instead.
- Inputs: link command with `-o` replaced by a fresh filename.
- Outputs: fresh-named executable that links and runs.
- Cautions: this only unblocks running under the new name; the canonical binary remains stale/locked, so the original build must still be retried after the lock clears for any deliverable that requires the canonical path.
- Preserve: sources, objects, and flags identical to the canonical link.
- Next: after running the fresh binary, return to Step 2–4 to restore the canonical output when it is required.

## Decision Rules
### When the error is LNK1105 with `error code 1224`
Treat the output `.exe` as locked by a running process (or a not-yet-released handle). Skip compiler-flag and source investigation entirely; go to process termination (Step 2).

### When a name-based kill returns no output / the lock persists
Enumerate processes by path or partial name match (`Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*<name>*' }`) and kill the matches; background launchers that `Wait` on the binary can hold the handle under a different process name. Observed in this group: a background `-Wait` process kept `dmls.exe` locked after `Stop-Process -Name dmls` had already run.

### When the relink immediately after a kill still reports LNK1105
Wait ~1 second and re-run the same build command; handle release can lag process exit. Observed: `Stop-Process -Name yggdrasil ...; make` still failed with LNK1105, while `Start-Sleep -Seconds 1; make` then linked successfully.

### When no matching process exists but the file still cannot be closed
Force-delete the output file (`Remove-Item -Force <path> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, check `$?`) and relink; a successful delete (`$? == True`) means the build system can recreate the file.

### When the canonical output must remain locked (e.g. a hung test binary cannot be killed) and a runnable binary is needed now
Link to a fresh output filename with the same sources/objects and run that instead; return to restoring the canonical name later. Observed: `test_solver2025.exe` / `test_indexing2025.exe` linked with exit 0 while the canonical `.exe` was still locked.

### When the relink succeeds but the binary then exits abnormally
Stop treating it as LNK1105 — the lock problem is solved; report the runtime failure separately (in this group, a test binary linked fine and then exited `-1073741571`, a stack-overflow crash unrelated to the lock).

## Invariants
- Never modify source files, build scripts, compiler flags, or object lists to "fix" LNK1105; the fault is a file lock, not the build definition.
- Only terminate processes whose name or path matches the locked output binary; do not kill unrelated processes or the whole shell session.
- Do not report build success without a fresh link log showing the original command completing with no `LNK1105`.
- Do not treat the existence of an old `.exe` as proof of a successful relink — the file may be a stale, still-locked binary from a previous build.
- Re-run the identical build command for verification; a link under a different output name only proves the workaround branch, not that the canonical target is buildable.
- Do not claim the lock is gone because a kill command was silent — `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`/`2>/dev/null` suppress both "killed" and "not found".
- Distinguish the lock problem from any subsequent runtime failure of the produced binary; report them separately.

## Common Failures
### Failure: name-based kill silently does nothing
- Symptoms: `Stop-Process -Name <x> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; make` prints nothing extra and the very next link still fails with LNK1105/1224.
- Causes: the holder's process name differs from the output name (launcher/`-Wait` parent, test harness, IDE), or no such named process exists so the kill was a no-op.
- Recovery: enumerate by path pattern (`Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*<name>*' -or $_.Name -like '*<name>*' }`), kill the matches, wait ~1 s, relink. If nothing matches, go to the delete branch.

### Failure: relink retried too quickly after a successful kill
- Symptoms: kill appears to work but the immediate relink still reports `error code 1224`.
- Causes: the OS releases the image file handle slightly after process termination.
- Recovery: `Start-Sleep -Seconds 1` (or `sleep 1`) and re-run the same build command; observed to succeed where the immediate retry failed.

### Failure: file locked but not deletable and no owning process found
- Symptoms: `Remove-Item -Force` fails and `Get-Process` by name/path returns nothing.
- Causes: unknown holder (driver-level or non-enumerable handle); the trace did not confirm a cause in this situation.
- Recovery: use the fresh-output-filename workaround to get a runnable binary, keep the canonical build reported as blocked, and escalate rather than deleting unrelated files.

### Failure: stale binary mistaken for a successful rebuild
- Symptoms: the `.exe` exists and runs, but it is the pre-lock version (e.g. a test binary that was crashing before the change).
- Causes: assuming existence equals a fresh link.
- Recovery: require a link log from the post-fix run of the original command; compare timestamps or content before claiming success.

### Failure: LNK1105 resolved but the binary crashes on run
- Symptoms: link succeeds, then the program exits with a crash code (e.g. `-1073741571`) or no output.
- Causes: unrelated runtime defect (in this group, a stack-overflow crash from large on-stack test fixtures).
- Recovery: stop LNK1105 work here — the lock is fixed — and handle the runtime failure as its own problem.

- The original build command's output contains no `LNK1105` and no `error code 1224`.
- The build's own success indicator appears (e.g. a `"Built: <path>"` line from the build script, `make` exiting 0, or the script's `Built build\<name>.exe` banner).
- The output file exists at the expected path (e.g. `[System.IO.File]::Exists('<path>')` → `True`, or the build script reports it).
- If a process kill was performed, a re-query shows no remaining process matching the output name/path (`Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Name -like '*<name>*' }` returns empty).
- If the original task requires running the binary, the produced executable launches and emits its expected output (e.g. test summary lines, application startup log) with a normal exit status.
- If only the fresh-filename workaround succeeded, the report explicitly states the canonical output is still blocked and must be relinked later.

### Example 1: kill test binaries by image name, wait, rebuild (Bash on Windows)
- Input: `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file 'build\frost_smoke.exe'; error code 1224` while `make CC=clang AR=llvm-ar OPT="-O0" BUILD=build` linked smoke/subsystem/bytecode test executables.

- Expected result: link completes, `make` runs the tests, log ends with `All smoke tests PASSED.` and `Results: 135 passed, 0 failed`.
- Parameterized values: image names = the three test executables; wait = `sleep 1`; build command = project `make` with its `CC/AR/OPT/BUILD` variables.

### Example 2: immediate retry fails, delayed retry succeeds (PowerShell)
- Input: `Stop-Process -Name yggdrasil -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; make 2>&1` still returned `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file 'bin\yggdrasil.exe'; error code 1224`.
- Procedure: treat as handle-release lag (Step 3/4 retry branch) → `Start-Sleep -Seconds 1; make 2>&1`.
- Expected result: the relinked binary builds and the log ends with `"Built: bin/yggdrasil.exe"`.
- Parameterized values: process name = `yggdrasil`; wait = 1 second; output = `bin\yggdrasil.exe`.

### Example 3: find holder by path, delete the locked file, full rebuild (PowerShell)
- Input: `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file 'D:\DMLS\build\dmls.exe'; error code 1224` persisted after `Stop-Process -Name dmls -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; ... .\build.bat run`.

- Parameterized values: path pattern = `*DMLS*`/`*dmls*`; output = `D:\DMLS\build\dmls.exe`; build command = `.\build.bat run`.

### Example 4: fresh output filename to unblock immediately (PowerShell)
- Input: `LINK : fatal error LNK1105: cannot close file 'build\tests\test_indexing.exe'; error code 1224` (a still-running/crashed test binary held the canonical name).

- Parameterized values: fresh suffix = `2025`; sources/objects unchanged from the canonical link.

- Actions: kill processes by expected image name first, e.g. PowerShell `Stop-Process -Name yggdrasil -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, or Bash `taskkill /F /IM frost_smoke.exe /IM frost_subsystems.exe 2>/dev/null`. If the name-based kill finds nothing or the lock persists, enumerate by path pattern, e.g. `Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*dmls*' -or $_.Name -like '*dmls*' } | Stop-Process -Force -EA 0`, then kill it.
- Inputs: output image name; shell type.
- Outputs: a process list (possibly empty) and terminated matching processes.
- Cautions: `Stop-Process -Name x -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` prints nothing when no such process exists — an empty result does not prove the lock is gone; check the file before relinking.
- Preserve: only processes whose name/path matches the locked output; never a blanket `Stop-Process` of everything.
- Next: proceed to Step 3.

### Step 3: Short wait, then verify the file handle is releasable
- Actions: sleep briefly (`Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500` / `sleep 1`), then optionally test deletability with `Remove-Item -Force <path> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` and check `$?`, or check existence with `[System.IO.File]::Exists('<path>')`.
- Inputs: locked output path.
- Outputs: whether the output file can now be deleted / exists.
- Cautions: Windows may keep the handle a moment after process exit — an immediate relink can still fail even after a successful kill.
- Preserve: if `Remove-Item` returns `True`, the file is gone; the build system will recreate it.
- Next: proceed to Step 4; if deletion fails and no matching process exists, use the Step 5 workaround.

### Step 4: Re-run the identical build command
- Actions: re-run the exact command from Step 1 (e.g. `make`, `.\build.bat run`, or the direct `clang++ ... -o <out>` line).
- Inputs: original build command.
- Outputs: new link log.
- Cautions: one retry immediately after a kill may still report LNK1105; retry once more after another ~1 s wait before escalating.
- Preserve: all flags, object lists, and output paths unchanged — this is verification of the lock fix, not a build-system refactor.
- Next: if the log contains no LNK1105 and the build's success message appears, go to Verification; if it still fails, go to Step 5.

### Step 5 (workaround): Link to a fresh output filename
- Actions: when the canonical output must stay locked or the lock cannot be cleared, relink with a different `-o` target (e.g. `build\tests\test_solver2025.exe`, `build\tests\test_indexing2025.exe`) using the same sources and objects; run that binary instead.
- Inputs: link command with `-o` replaced by a fresh filename.
- Outputs: fresh-named executable that links and runs.
- Cautions: this only unblocks running under the new name; the canonical binary remains stale/locked, so the original build must still be retried after the lock clears for any deliverable that requires the canonical path.
- Preserve: sources, objects, and flags identical to the canonical link.
- Next: after running the fresh binary, return to Step 2–4 to restore the canonical output when it is required.

## Decision Rules
### When the error is LNK1105 with `error code 1224`
Treat the output `.exe` as locked by a running process (or a not-yet-released handle). Skip compiler-flag and source investigation entirely; go to process termination (Step 2).

### When a name-based kill returns no output / the lock persists
Enumerate processes by path or partial name match (`Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*<name>*' }`) and kill the matches; background launchers that `Wait` on the binary can hold the handle under a different process name. Observed in this group: a background `-Wait` process kept `dmls.exe` locked after `Stop-Process -Name dmls` had already run.

### When the relink immediately after a kill still reports LNK1105
Wait ~1 second and re-run the same build command; handle release can lag process exit. Observed: `Stop-Process -Name yggdrasil ...; make` still failed with LNK1105, while `Start-Sleep -Seconds 1; make` then linked successfully.

### When no matching process exists but the file still cannot be closed
Force-delete the output file (`Remove-Item -Force <path> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, check `$?`) and relink; a successful delete (`$? == True`) means the build system can recreate the file.

### When the canonical output must remain locked (e.g. a hung test binary cannot be killed) and a runnable binary is needed now
Link to a fresh output filename with the same sources/objects and run that instead; return to restoring the canonical name later. Observed: `test_solver2025.exe` / `test_indexing2025.exe` linked with exit 0 while the canonical `.exe` was still locked.

### When the relink succeeds but the binary then exits abnormally
Stop treating it as LNK1105 — the lock problem is solved; report the runtime failure separately (in this group, a test binary linked fine and then exited `-1073741571`, a stack-overflow crash unrelated to the lock).

## Invariants
- Never modify source files, build scripts, compiler flags, or object lists to "fix" LNK1105; the fault is a file lock, not the build definition.
- Only terminate processes whose name or path matches the locked output binary; do not kill unrelated processes or the whole shell session.
- Do not report build success without a fresh link log showing the original command completing with no `LNK1105`.
- Do not treat the existence of an old `.exe` as proof of a successful relink — the file may be a stale, still-locked binary from a previous build.
- Re-run the identical build command for verification; a link under a different output name only proves the workaround branch, not that the canonical target is buildable.
- Do not claim the lock is gone because a kill command was silent — `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`/`2>/dev/null` suppress both "killed" and "not found".
- Distinguish the lock problem from any subsequent runtime failure of the produced binary; report them separately.

## Common Failures
### Failure: name-based kill silently does nothing
- Symptoms: `Stop-Process -Name <x> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; make` prints nothing extra and the very next link still fails with LNK1105/1224.
- Causes: the holder's process name differs from the output name (launcher/`-Wait` parent, test harness, IDE), or no such named process exists so the kill was a no-op.
- Recovery: enumerate by path pattern (`Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*<name>*' -or $_.Name -like '*<name>*' }`), kill the matches, wait ~1 s, relink. If nothing matches, go to the delete branch.

### Failure: relink retried too quickly after a successful kill
- Symptoms: kill appears to work but the immediate relink still reports `error code 1224`.
- Causes: the OS releases the image file handle slightly after process termination.
- Recovery: `Start-Sleep -Seconds 1` (or `sleep 1`) and re-run the same build command; observed to succeed where the immediate retry failed.

### Failure: file locked but not deletable and no owning process found
- Symptoms: `Remove-Item -Force` fails and `Get-Process` by name/path returns nothing.
- Causes: unknown holder (driver-level or non-enumerable handle); the trace did not confirm a cause in this situation.
- Recovery: use the fresh-output-filename workaround to get a runnable binary, keep the canonical build reported as blocked, and escalate rather than deleting unrelated files.

### Failure: stale binary mistaken for a successful rebuild
- Symptoms: the `.exe` exists and runs, but it is the pre-lock version (e.g. a test binary that was crashing before the change).
- Causes: assuming existence equals a fresh link.
- Recovery: require a link log from the post-fix run of the original command; compare timestamps or content before claiming success.

### Failure: LNK1105 resolved but the binary crashes on run
- Symptoms: link succeeds, then the program exits with a crash code (e.g. `-1073741571`) or no output.
- Causes: unrelated runtime defect (in this group, a stack-overflow crash from large on-stack test fixtures).
- Recovery: stop LNK1105 work here — the lock is fixed — and handle the runtime failure as its own problem.

## Verification
Check each item against a fresh tool result from the post-fix run (do not mark based on memory or on the pre-fix log):
- The original build command's output contains no `LNK1105` and no `error code 1224`.
- The build's own success indicator appears (e.g. a `"Built: <path>"` line from the build script, `make` exiting 0, or the script's `Built build\<name>.exe` banner).
- The output file exists at the expected path (e.g. `[System.IO.File]::Exists('<path>')` → `True`, or the build script reports it).

- If the original task requires running the binary, the produced executable launches and emits its expected output (e.g. test summary lines, application startup log) with a normal exit status.
- If only the fresh-filename workaround succeeded, the report explicitly states the canonical output is still blocked and must be relinked later.

# Fix LNK2019 unresolved external for header-declared globals with inline variables

## Goal
Resolve LNK2019/unresolved-external errors for a global variable that is declared `extern` in a shared header but defined only in one translation unit (typically main.cpp) that is excluded from secondary binaries such as test executables, by making the header the single definition site.

## Scope
### In scope
- Link failures naming an unresolved data symbol (e.g. `error LNK2019: unresolved external symbol "int g_verbose"`) referenced from code compiled into test binaries.
- Converting the header declaration to an inline variable definition (`inline int g_verbose = 0;`) and deleting the now-duplicate definition from the former defining translation unit.
- Verifying by rebuilding both the test binaries and the main program.

### Out of scope
- Function-level unresolved externals caused by missing source files in the link line (fix by adding the file, not by inlining).
- Symbol name/mangling mismatches between declaration and definition.
- Constants better expressed as `constexpr`.

## Inputs
- Linker error output (string): required; must contain `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol` plus the mangled/unmangled symbol name; the referencing object (e.g. `solver-*.o`) tells you which translation unit needs it.
- Header file declaring the global (file path, e.g. `include/log.hpp`): required.
- Defining translation unit (file path, e.g. `main.cpp`) that is compiled into the main program but not into the test binaries: required.
- Build/link command for the secondary binaries (the test build script): required; no default.
- No defaults for the above.

## Outputs
### Artifacts
- Edited header where the global is defined as `inline T name = <initializer>;`.
- Edited former defining .cpp with the duplicate definition removed.

### Success criteria
- Every binary links: test executables no longer report LNK2019 for the symbol, and the main program still builds and runs (no duplicate-definition/multiple-definition errors).

### Failure criteria
- Multiple-definition errors at link time (old definition not removed).
- The main program's behavior changes because the variable's value is no longer set as before.

## Preconditions
- The error is a data or function symbol that is genuinely defined in exactly one .cpp that the failing binary does not link (confirmed by reading the header's `extern` declaration and the .cpp definition).
- You know which binaries exclude that .cpp (here: test binaries link the engine/parser/internals sources plus repl.cpp but not main.cpp).
- You can rebuild both the secondary binaries and the main program to check both directions.
- If the main program is currently running and holds its own executable open on Windows, terminate it before relinking.

## Procedure
### Step 1: Confirm the symbol's single definition sits in an excluded translation unit
- Actions: Read the header to find `extern T name;` and grep the sources for its definition. If the only definition is in a file not part of the failing binary's link line (e.g. main.cpp excluded from test builds), that is the cause.
- Inputs: linker output, header, sources.
- Outputs: confirmed diagnosis.
- Cautions: if the symbol is a function, prefer adding the source file to the link over any header trick.
- Preserve: the variable's name, type, and initializer semantics.
- Next: proceed to Step 2.

### Step 2: Convert to an inline variable in the header
- Actions: Replace `extern int g_verbose;` with `inline int g_verbose = 0;` in the header (C++17 inline variables give one definition across all translation units).
- Inputs: header.
- Outputs: edited header.
- Cautions: keep the initializer identical to the old definition so runtime behavior is unchanged; `inline` works for variables of literal type only — do not use it for non-literal types.
- Preserve: all uses of the variable.
- Next: proceed to Step 3.

### Step 3: Remove the old definition
- Actions: Delete the now-redundant definition (e.g. `int g_verbose = 0;`) from the former defining .cpp file.
- Inputs: defining .cpp.
- Outputs: edited file.
- Cautions: leaving it causes a multiple-definition link error on toolchains that do not treat it as the inline definition.
- Preserve: everything else in that file, including `main`.
- Next: rebuild everything.

### Step 4: Verify both kinds of binary
- Actions: Rebuild the test binaries and confirm the symbol error is gone and tests run; rebuild/run the main program to confirm it still works and that any code that sets the variable (e.g. a --verbose flag) still behaves.
- Inputs: build commands for both.
- Outputs: link/run results.
- Cautions: a locked output binary on Windows (`LNK1105`) is environmental; kill the stale process and retry.
- Next: stop when both build and run cleanly.

## Decision Rules
### When the unresolved symbol is a global variable declared extern in a header and defined in exactly one excluded .cpp
Replace the header declaration with an inline variable definition and delete the .cpp definition.

### When the unresolved symbol is a function
Do not inline it via the header; add the defining source file to the failing binary's link line instead.

### When the build now reports a multiple-definition error for the same symbol
The old definition was not removed (Step 3 incomplete); remove it rather than reverting the header.

### When the failing binary links every source except the one defining the symbol and adding that source would drag in main()
Prefer the inline-variable route: it avoids duplicate `main` and keeps the binary's source list minimal.

## Invariants
- The variable keeps its exact name, type, and initializer so observable behavior is unchanged in every binary.
- Exactly one definition conceptually exists: the inline definition in the header; the previous .cpp definition is deleted, not commented out or guarded.
- Both the secondary binaries (tests) and the primary program are rebuilt after the change; fixing one at the expense of the other is not acceptable.
- No unrelated source files are added to link lines as part of this fix.

## Common Failures
### Failure: LNK2019 persists for the data symbol in every test binary
- Symptoms: `error LNK2019: unresolved external symbol "int g_verbose" ... referenced in function "void __cdecl vlog(...)"` on each test link.
- Causes: the only definition lived in main.cpp, which test binaries do not link.
- Recovery: inline-variable definition in the header plus removal of the old definition.

### Failure: multiple-definition error after the header change
- Symptoms: the main program now fails to link with a duplicate symbol for the same name.
- Causes: the .cpp definition was left in place.
- Recovery: delete the old definition; do not remove the inline definition.

### Failure: behavior differs between the main program and tests
- Symptoms: verbose logging on in one binary, off in the other.
- Causes: the initializer in the header differs from the old definition, or the program's flag-setting path was disturbed.
- Recovery: restore the original initializer (`0`) and re-check the flag-handling code path in the main program.

## Verification
- Rebuild the test binaries: no LNK2019 mentions the symbol; each test binary links and starts.
- Run the test suites: they print PASS/FAIL lines as before (the fix must not alter engine behavior).
- Rebuild the main program: it links (proving no multiple definition) and still runs its acceptance scenario.
- Grep the sources: the symbol appears as an `inline` definition in exactly one header and nowhere else as a definition.

## Examples
### Example 1: verbose-logging flag unreachable from test binaries
- Input: `include/log.hpp` declares `extern int g_verbose;`, `vlog()` in the engine reads it, and only `main.cpp` defines `int g_verbose = 0;`. Every test link fails with `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol "int g_verbose"`.
- Procedure: replace the header declaration with `inline int g_verbose = 0;`, delete `int g_verbose = 0;` from main.cpp, rebuild tests and the main program.
- Expected result: tests link and run (in the trace the very next run compiled all suites and executed them, e.g. `22/22 tests passed` in the lexer suite); the main program still builds.
- Parameterized values: symbol `g_verbose`, type `int`, initializer `0`, header `include/log.hpp`, excluded TU `main.cpp`.

## Evidence
- problem — file_id `claude_code__c99032e9-377b-4ae9-a9a9-ec7752b059cd__segment-06`, source_index 975, source_part_index 0, quote: "solver-c181c1.o : error LNK2019: unresolved external symbol \"int g_verbose\" (?g_verbose@@3HA) referenced in function \"void __cdecl vlog(char const *,char const *,...)\" (?vlog@@YAXPEBD0ZZ)", supports: all seven test binaries failed to link for the same reason — the engine object referenced a global defined only in the unlinked main.cpp.
- action — same file_id, source_index 977, source_part_index 0, quote: "inline int g_verbose = 0;", supports: the header declaration `extern int g_verbose;` was replaced with an inline variable definition (same edit shows the old string in old_string).
- action — same file_id, source_index 981, source_part_index 0, quote: "int main", supports: the duplicate definition was removed from main.cpp by deleting `int g_verbose = 0;\n\n` immediately before `int main`.
- verification — same file_id, source_index 984, source_part_index 0, quote: "=== 2 suite(s) PASSED, 5 FAILED ===", supports: immediately after the change every test binary linked and executed (two suites fully passed; the remaining failures were runtime test issues, not link errors), confirming the LNK2019 was resolved for all suites.
